title: Chicken or Turkey Fricassee with Sauce, No Potatoes (Potatoes Served Separately), Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey fricassee is a tender braised meat dish cooked in a fragrant sauce made from tomatoes, onion, garlic, olive oil, and characteristic Puerto Rican spices: adobo, oregano, cumin, and fresh cilantro. The dish is served without potatoes; potatoes are offered on the side so diners can add them as they wish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puerto Rican cuisine blends Spanish, African, and Taíno influences, reflected in the bright flavor of fricassee.
The traditional fricassee sauce is simmered slowly, allowing the meat to fully absorb the spice aromas.
The original recipe often includes “pico de gallo,” a fresh salsa of tomatoes, onion, pepper, and lime, served alongside.
Chicken and turkey are frequently marinated in lime juice and olive oil before cooking, making the meat especially juicy.
The dish is commonly accompanied by rice, beans, and fried plantains (tostones) as side dishes.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Skin‑less poultry contains little saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamins B3, B6, and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Adobo, cumin, and fresh cilantro contain polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Lime juice and garlic boost immunity thanks to vitamin C and sulfur‑rich compounds.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If prepared with pre‑made seasoning mixes, the dish can be high in sodium; salt should be monitored.

items.title: Cross‑contamination
items.content: Preparing the fricassee alongside seafood or other allergens may lead to cross‑contamination.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Poultry must be cooked to a safe internal temperature to avoid salmonella or campylobacter infection.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fricassee hot, spooning the sauce over the meat. It pairs well with steamed rice, beans, fried plantains, or a fresh salad. Potatoes are served separately—boiled, roasted, or mashed—so each person can add them to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stovetop, adding a splash of broth or water to keep the sauce from drying out.
